title: Samsung Wants to Keep You Away from the Doctor with AI Health Tools
summary: Samsung is pushing AI-driven preventive health through Galaxy wearables, using algorithms to analyze trends and give personalized nudges. New features include overnight Vitals monitoring, wrist-based ECG reports and a photo-based AI nutrition tracker to spot early signs of illness. Samsung says AI processing is optional and that users retain full control of their data, while R&D leaders emphasize transparency and custodian-style handling of personal health information.
content:
Samsung is placing a major bet on AI tools to rethink healthtech, aiming to detect wellness issues before users need to visit a doctor. Rather than focusing on generic targets like 10,000 steps, the company is shifting toward personalized nudges and continuous trend analysis delivered by Galaxy watches and rings.

Annika Bizon, VP of Product and Marketing for Mobile Experience, told TechRadar that Samsung’s new approach uses algorithms to analyze daily body trends and generate actionable guidance in real time. A key example is the Vitals feature, which monitors overnight heart rate and breathing patterns to flag possible early signs of illness, such as an oncoming cold, so users can rest or take precautions sooner.

Samsung is also expanding medical-grade capabilities at the wrist. Built-in ECG tools can produce detailed reports, and an upcoming AI nutrition feature promises quick meal logging by analyzing a photo of a plate. These tools are intended to help users notice subtle shifts in health baselines that traditional activity metrics can miss.

Privacy and data control remain central to Samsung’s pitch. Bizon stressed that using AI features is optional and that Samsung Health will work without enabling AI. Rohit Ali from Samsung R&D UK reiterated that the company positions itself as a custodian, not an owner, of user data. While opting out preserves privacy, unlocking the most predictive features requires permitting the AI to learn an individual’s baseline patterns.

Samsung acknowledges that convincing people to share sensitive health data hinges on total transparency and clear value from the insights provided. Executives say the company must demonstrate that predictive, personalized signals are worth the tradeoff for users who choose to opt in.
